discernible

dih-SUR-nuh-bul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Discernible is able to be perceived, recognized, or made out clearly, especially with careful attention.

Only after the conservator cleaned three centuries of grime from the canvas did the artist's faint, original signature finally become discernible in the corner.

Worked Example

To the untrained ear, the twins' voices sounded identical, but their music teacher insisted a discernible difference existed in how each one held a high note.

Discernible describes something that can be noticed or told apart, often only with careful attention -- it isn't always obvious at first glance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

noticeable: Noticeable describes what strikes you without any special effort -- a noticeable stain or a noticeable noise announces itself. A discernible detail is quieter: it can be made out, but often only when you give it a careful, deliberate look.

perceptible: Perceptible means able to be registered by the senses at all -- a perceptible tremor or scent may sit right at the edge of detection. Discernible adds recognition: a discernible feature can not only be sensed but actually made out and identified for what it is.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hidden: kept out of sight, so it cannot be seen or noticed

indiscernible: impossible to make out or distinguish clearly

Where it sits · how surely it can be picked out — faint → discernible → unmistakable

faint vs. discernible: Faint just means weak or slight -- it doesn't necessarily say whether the thing can actually be identified, the way discernible does.

unmistakable vs. discernible: Unmistakable goes even further than discernible, describing something so clear it couldn't possibly be confused with anything else.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — dis-

prefix — dis-: apart (Latin)

root — cern-

root — cern-: to separate, sift, perceive (Latin cernere)

suffix — -ible

suffix — -ible: able to be (Latin -ibilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Discernible comes from Latin dis- ('apart') + cernere ('to separate, sift, perceive') -- the same root behind ascertain, which you already met in Part 2 of this course. To discern something is to 'sift it apart' from everything around it; if you can do that, it's discernible. Notice the spelling, too: discern is already a real English word, yet it still takes -ible rather than -able -- another of this unit's exceptions.

Use the root in a new word: ascertain

Use the root in a new word: ascertain: Investigators worked for weeks to ascertain the exact cause of the fire.
